screens.title: Sending Data to the Cloud
screens.narratorSegment: When your Raspberry Pi collects sensor readings, the next step is often storing and viewing that information remotely. Cloud platforms let you log readings, visualize trends, and trigger alerts without keeping everything on the Pi. In beginner projects, services such as ThingSpeak or Adafruit IO accept simple HTTP requests so your Pi can push data directly. For larger systems you can use a custom endpoint or an enterprise IoT service. This lesson will show the common pattern: read the sensor, format the measurement, send an HTTP request, and confirm the cloud stored the value. We will walk through a ready-made example that uses a simple GET request, discuss the rate limits you may hit, and explain how to protect A P I keys and use HTTPS. By the end you will understand which cloud option fits a hobby project versus a production setup, and you will be prepared to try the hands-on task of creating a channel and sending live data. Think about one sensor you have available now and how seeing its history online could help you notice trends or faults.

screens.title: Why store sensor data in the cloud?
screens.narratorSegment: Storing sensor data in the cloud changes what you can do with measurements. Locally on the Pi you can log values, but the cloud makes that history accessible from any device, lets you visualize trends over days or months, and enables alerts when values cross thresholds. For example, a temperature sensor on a greenhouse can trigger a notification if the reading stays above a limit, and historical plots can show seasonal changes. The trade-offs are also important: you add network dependency, potential costs, and the need to manage credentials and rate limits. A common beginner mistake is assuming unlimited updates; ThingSpeak and similar services often limit free accounts to one update every 15 seconds. That means your script should respect rate limits to avoid dropped updates or account restrictions. Think of the cloud as a secure, shared notebook: it stores measurements, keeps a time-ordered record, and can share that record with dashboards or other services. When deciding to use the cloud, ask what you gain—remote access, alerting, or integration—and weigh it against the operational complexity and privacy requirements. How would your project change if you could view its data from your phone?

screens.title: Choosing a platform: ThingSpeak, Adafruit IO, or custom
screens.narratorSegment: When selecting where to send data, think about the balance between simplicity and control. ThingSpeak is built for simple HTTP logging and quick plots; it accepts straightforward GET or POST calls so you can move from sensor to plot in minutes. Adafruit IO adds more GUI-friendly feeds and dashboards tailored to makers and integrates with other Adafruit services. A custom endpoint, typically a small Flask app or a database you host, gives you maximum control: you choose the data format, authentication, storage duration, and integrations, but you also take on the responsibility for uptime, backups, and security. For a first project, ThingSpeak or Adafruit IO are excellent because they remove server administration. If you later need custom processing, a self-hosted Flask receiver or cloud virtual machine can accept JSON and forward records into a database. Consider also scale and rate limits: free tiers may restrict updates and retention. The right choice depends on whether you value speed of setup, dashboard polish, or full control over data and code. Which trade-off matters more for your project? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Sending data to ThingSpeak — example script
screens.narratorSegment: A common beginner pattern uses a small loop on the Pi that reads a sensor, formats the value, and sends an HTTP request to the cloud. The example script uses the requests library to issue an HTTP GET where the A P I key and the field value are included in the request. In practice the script reads the sensor, multiplies or formats values as needed, and sleeps between sends so it respects service rate limits. The important behaviour to notice is the network call and error handling: the script tries the request, prints the response code for confirmation, and catches network exceptions to avoid crashing. For ThingSpeak specifically, free accounts allow an update roughly every 15 seconds, so many examples sleep for twenty seconds between sends. When you move to production, convert the A P I key into an environment variable and use HTTPS endpoints only. Try running the script once to confirm a successful response, then monitor the ThingSpeak dashboard to confirm values appear. What would you log to detect a missed send and why? content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › ThingSpeak example
Example script (visual)
import requests
from time import sleep
from gpiozero import DistanceSensor

API_KEY = "YOUR_THINGSPEAK_API_KEY"
sensor = DistanceSensor(echo=24, trigger=23)

while True:
    distance = sensor.distance * 100
    url = f"https://api.thingspeak.com/update?api_key={API_KEY}&field1={distance:.1f}"
    try:
        response = requests.get(url, timeout=10)
        print(f"Sent: {distance:.1f} cm, response: {response.status_code}")
    except requests.RequestException as e:
        print(f"Error: {e}")
    sleep(20)
Note: the code above is a learning example. Move keys out of the script before sharing.
What to watch for
  • Formatting: round or format values to reduce payload size.
  • Error handling: catch network exceptions so the loop continues.
  • Rate limits: sleep longer than the service minimum update interval.
Key Takeaway

A simple HTTP call with basic error handling is enough to reliably push sensor values to ThingSpeak for hobby projects.

Security tip: do not keep the API key in plain text in a public script.

screens.title: The general send pattern
screens.narratorSegment: There is a compact, repeatable process for sending sensor data to any cloud endpoint. First, read the sensor and convert the raw reading into a human-friendly unit. For example, multiply a distance sensor's fraction by one hundred to get centimeters. Second, format the reading—either include it as a query parameter in a GET request for simple services, or build a JSON payload and send it with an HTTP POST when the receiver expects structured data. Third, send the HTTP request and wait for the response. Check response codes to confirm success and record the timestamp if needed. Fourth, handle failure: retry sensibly, log the error, and avoid tight retry loops that flood the network. Finally, sleep between sends to respect rate limits and conserve bandwidth. A practical tip is to add small debug logs showing the sent value and the server response so you can diagnose issues quickly. Practice this pattern until it becomes second nature: reading, formatting, sending, confirming, and then waiting. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Creating a custom Flask receiver
screens.narratorSegment: Sometimes you want complete control over how data is received and stored. A minimal Flask server can run on another Pi or a cloud VM and accept JSON payloads from your device. The receiver route extracts the JSON, performs lightweight validation, prints or stores the data, and returns a simple success message. This approach gives you flexibility to add authentication, custom processing, or direct insertion into a database. However, it also requires you to manage hosting, ensure the server is reachable, and implement secure transport with HTTPS if exposed to the public internet. When you migrate to production, use environment variables for any secrets, enable basic request validation, and run the server behind a reverse proxy or a managed TLS endpoint to provide HTTPS. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Flask receiver
Minimal Flask server (visual)
from flask import Flask, request

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/data", methods=["POST"])
def receive_data():
    data = request.json
    print(data)
    return {"status": "ok"}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000)
This example prints the JSON payload to the server console. Add validation and storage for real projects.
Practical notes
  • Use POST with JSON when the receiver expects structured data.
  • Add simple validation to check required fields before storage.
  • Host behind HTTPS or a reverse proxy to protect transport.
Common pitfall

Exposing a development server to the public without TLS or authentication can leak data or allow misuse. Harden before production.

screens.title: HTTP GET vs POST for data logging
screens.narratorSegment: Two common HTTP approaches are GET with query parameters and POST with a JSON body. GET is simple and often used by beginner services like ThingSpeak where you include the A P I key and field value as part of the request URL. It is convenient for quick logging and when the cloud A P I is designed to accept query-based updates. POST with JSON is preferred when you need structured data, multiple fields, nested objects, or when you want cleaner separation of credentials and payload. POST also avoids very long URLs and is more aligned with typical RESTful design for creating resources. The practical difference is how the receiver parses the incoming data: a GET-based service reads fields from the URL, while a POST receiver reads JSON from the request body. A useful rule of thumb: use GET for single simple fields on trusted endpoints; use POST and JSON for any multi-field payloads or when you control the receiver. Always check the service documentation to match its expected method, and test a single well-formed request before putting the script into a loop.

GET with query parameters
Simple, visible in the URL, suitable for single fields and quick services like ThingSpeak.
Pros
  • Very easy to construct.
  • No body parsing required on simple receivers.
Cons
  • URL length limits and visible parameters.
  • Less suitable for complex, multi-field payloads.
POST with JSON
Structured payloads in the request body, better for multiple values or nested data.

  • Slightly more code to build and parse the JSON body.
  • Requires correct content-type handling on the receiver.
Key Takeaway

Match the HTTP method to the receiver's expectations: simple single values can use GET, structured data should use POST with JSON.

screens.title: JSON payloads and formatting
screens.narratorSegment: JSON is the common format for structured data when sending multi-field readings. A good JSON payload includes clear field names, consistent units, and a timestamp if the receiver doesn't add one. For example, send temperature in degrees Celsius under a field named temperature and include an ISO-style timestamp or rely on the receiver to add server time. Keep payloads compact: avoid sending repeated metadata with every reading if the receiver already knows the device identity. Validate the payload on the server side to guard against malformed data. On the Pi, build a dictionary of keys and values, then use the JSON module or the requests library's JSON parameter to send the payload; that ensures correct content-type headers. A common mistake is mixing units or inconsistent field names across sends. Decide on a simple schema early and stick to it to make later analysis much easier. What fields will you include in your first payload and why? JSON payloads and formatting means use consistent field names, units, and include a timestamp; validate incoming json to avoid bad records.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: API keys, HTTPS, and credential safety
screens.narratorSegment: Security is essential when sending data or using cloud services. A P I keys grant authority to write data or access features; if leaked, someone else can use your account. Never hard-code keys into scripts that you store in public repositories. Instead, store keys in environment variables or configuration files excluded from version control. On the Pi, create a local. env file and load it at runtime with a small library or use the operating system environment. Always use HTTPS endpoints so your A P I key and payload travel encrypted across the network. For a custom Flask endpoint, protect write operations with long random tokens or basic authentication, and consider additional validation on the server. Another common oversight is logging keys to debug output; avoid printing secrets. A simple verification exercise: move a key out of a sample script into an environment variable and confirm the script still sends data. screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting checklist
screens.narratorSegment: When a send fails, a focused checklist makes debugging quick. First, check the network: does the Pi have internet connectivity and DNS resolution? Second, inspect the A P I key: is it present, correct, and not accidentally truncated when stored as an environment variable? A frequent error is missing or malformed keys because of stray quotes or line breaks. Third, verify the request method and payload match the service expectations—GET versus POST and query parameters versus JSON. Fourth, look at response codes and any returned error message; the status code is the fastest clue. Fifth, confirm you are respecting rate limits; if you send too often, the service may drop requests silently or return a specific error. Sixth, watch for exceptions in your script; capture and write them to a local log for later review. Finally, if using a custom server, check server logs to see if the POST reached it and whether validation rejected it. Use these steps as a debugging routine so you can isolate the issue quickly and iterate toward a successful send. fullNarratorScript:
When your Raspberry Pi collects sensor readings, the next step is often storing and viewing that information remotely. Cloud platforms let you log readings, visualize trends, and trigger alerts without keeping everything on the Pi. In beginner projects, services such as ThingSpeak or Adafruit IO accept simple HTTP requests so your Pi can push data directly. For larger systems you can use a custom endpoint or an enterprise IoT service. This lesson will show the common pattern: read the sensor, format the measurement, send an HTTP request, and confirm the cloud stored the value. We will walk through a ready-made example that uses a simple GET request, discuss the rate limits you may hit, and explain how to protect A P I keys and use HTTPS. By the end you will understand which cloud option fits a hobby project versus a production setup, and you will be prepared to try the hands-on task of creating a channel and sending live data. Think about one sensor you have available now and how seeing its history online could help you notice trends or faults.

This lesson has four clear objectives that move from recognition to practical application. First, you will identify beginner-friendly cloud platforms and understand their role for IoT data storage and visualization. Knowing the platform landscape helps you pick a tool that fits a hobby project or a growing system. Second, you will be able to send sensor data using HTTP requests from Python on the Pi. That is a hands-on skill: formatting a value and making the network call. Third, you will learn to use concrete services such as ThingSpeak and Adafruit IO, and you will also see how a custom Flask endpoint can receive JSON from the Pi. This helps when you need greater control. Fourth, you will discuss the role of A P I keys, HTTPS, and basic credential security. You will learn practical steps like using environment variables and avoiding public commits. Each objective includes a small visual mnemonic so you can remember the skill and a verified competency milestone to check your progress.

This second objectives slide frames the same four goals as practical tasks so you can measure progress. First, when you identify cloud platforms, try creating a free account and exploring a dashboard; that hands-on check helps you see the limits and strengths. Second, when learning to send data using HTTP, your success is sending a single field value and observing a successful response code from the service. Third, when using ThingSpeak, Adafruit IO, or a Flask endpoint, practice by creating a channel or a minimal server and verify that incoming data appears or prints on the receiver. Fourth, for A P I keys and HTTPS, your milestone is moving a key out of your script into an environment variable and confirming the request still works. Each objective includes a short mnemonic to help remember the action and a micro-verification step you can perform in ten minutes or less.

Storing sensor data in the cloud changes what you can do with measurements. Locally on the Pi you can log values, but the cloud makes that history accessible from any device, lets you visualize trends over days or months, and enables alerts when values cross thresholds. For example, a temperature sensor on a greenhouse can trigger a notification if the reading stays above a limit, and historical plots can show seasonal changes. The trade-offs are also important: you add network dependency, potential costs, and the need to manage credentials and rate limits. A common beginner mistake is assuming unlimited updates; ThingSpeak and similar services often limit free accounts to one update every 15 seconds. That means your script should respect rate limits to avoid dropped updates or account restrictions. Think of the cloud as a secure, shared notebook: it stores measurements, keeps a time-ordered record, and can share that record with dashboards or other services. When deciding to use the cloud, ask what you gain—remote access, alerting, or integration—and weigh it against the operational complexity and privacy requirements. How would your project change if you could view its data from your phone?

When selecting where to send data, think about the balance between simplicity and control. ThingSpeak is built for simple HTTP logging and quick plots; it accepts straightforward GET or POST calls so you can move from sensor to plot in minutes. Adafruit IO adds more GUI-friendly feeds and dashboards tailored to makers and integrates with other Adafruit services. A custom endpoint, typically a small Flask app or a database you host, gives you maximum control: you choose the data format, authentication, storage duration, and integrations, but you also take on the responsibility for uptime, backups, and security. For a first project, ThingSpeak or Adafruit IO are excellent because they remove server administration. If you later need custom processing, a self-hosted Flask receiver or cloud virtual machine can accept JSON and forward records into a database. Consider also scale and rate limits: free tiers may restrict updates and retention. The right choice depends on whether you value speed of setup, dashboard polish, or full control over data and code.
